title: Contextual economics: reading digest + sprint notes
content:
Quick orientation (notes to self):

Purpose: synthesize recent papers + posts on how context management interacts with per-token cost/latency and draft a 1-week sprint plan to prototype a hybrid prefix-indexed KV cache that favors short, high-value prefixes for low-latency interactive apps. Keep it small: measurable metrics, reproducible configs, and a simple A/B on p95 latency + token cost.

What I read (short summary + takeaways)
1) Sparse cross-window attention + cache sketches (paper: sparse-cross-window-2026) — arXiv
   - Problem: full-attention over long windows is expensive; authors propose a sketching layer that pre-selects candidate key blocks across previous segments.
   - Takeaways: selection can be done cheaply (hash-based) and reduces KV reads by ~6x in their sim. But quality depends on selection recall.
   - Notes: this aligns with our desire to reduce token reads at tail of sessions. Could combine with frequency-based prefix heuristics.

2) Prefix-indexed KV cache (blog + GitHub PR)
   - Short summary: index prefixes (n-grams or rolling hashes) to map to cached KV fragments; lookups are O(1) average and enable partial reuse for rephrased prompts.
   - Takeaways: overhead is memory and index maintenance; eviction policy matters (LRU vs freq-based). Good match for interactive UIs where the same leading context repeats.

3) Edge cost-curves and batching vs latency (engineering blog, 2026-09)
   - Summary: batching saves GPU cycles but increases tail latency for bursty interactive workloads. They present a break-even graph for batch size vs p95 latency at various request rates.
   - Takeaways: for hosted interactive endpoints we need adaptive batching that collapses when request arrival is sparse. This motivates keeping a low-overhead cache to reduce per-request token generation rather than relying only on batching.

Conference takeaways (OSDI-style workshop notes)
- People are experimenting with multi-tier caches (on-device short-term + server-side dense cache). Good note: prioritize small, high-value prefixes on-device.
- Evaluation is drifting toward user-centric metrics: completion time perceived by user, rather than raw p50 latency. For our experiments, track perceived latency proxy — e.g., time-to-first-byte + initial token inter-arrival.

Open questions / hypotheses (to test)
- H1: A small prefix-indexed KV cache (top-500 prefixes per model) will cut average KV reads by 30–40% with <1% degradation in output quality on our interactive testset.
- H2: Combining frequency-based prefix ranking with sparse candidate selection increases recall without blowing up index size.
- H3: For bursts (<10 qps), a cache hit rate gain of 15% yields lower cost than a 2x batching strategy because of p95 latency inflation.

Experiment plan (week-long, minimal)
- Dataset: 2k interactive sessions sampled from staging logs (last 30 days), deduped, bucketed by session length and user percentiles. (Metric: hit rate by session decile)
- Implementations:
  A) baseline: no prefix index, existing KV cache read-all-keys for last N tokens
  B) prefix-indexed: store top-500 prefixes (rolling normalized n-gram hash) mapping to KV offsets; lookup returns candidate KV segments to read
  C) hybrid: B + sparse candidate rescoring (small LSH sketch)
- Eval metrics (for each run): p50/p95 latency, tokens read per request, server-side GPU token-cost estimate, ROUGE/EM-style fidelity on small prompt set, and a manual spot-check of hallucination rate for generation tasks. Also capture time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and tokens-per-second for throughput.
- Config knobs to record: prefix length (8/16 tokens), max candidates returned (1/3/5), eviction policy (LRU/lfu/score-based), quantized-KV enabled (yes/no).
- Success criteria: reduce tokens-read by >=25% on medium-length sessions (50–200 tokens) while p95 latency changes <+10% and automated fidelity delta <1% on key metrics.

Implementation notes (practicalities)
- Add a small adapter in the runtime path that performs prefix hashing pre-request (cheap CPU op). Hash must be canonicalized by token ids to avoid tokenization drift.
- Store index as memory-mapped file on host for Dedicated instances; for Hosted we can use in-memory sharded maps with periodic snapshots.
- Eviction: start with simple LFU with decay; measure skew in the first 24h.

Short-term TODOs (today / next 72h)
- [ ] sketch the prefix hash function and choose canonical tokenization (owner: me)
- [ ] prototype index lookup microbench (owner: Noah) — target <200us lookup for 3 candidates
- [ ] pick 2k sessions and produce the gold-set for fidelity checks (owner: Rina)
- [ ] open a draft PR with basic storage shim and config flags (owner: A. Khatri) — link to issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/proposals/issues/489

Notes-to-self (less formal)
- Watch out for tokenization drift between client and runtime: canonicalize on ingestion.
- Keep experiment small: push data collection early. If hit rates are low, don't escalate to complicated LSH until we have a deterministic failure analysis.
- Remember to log prefix collision rates and prefix-to-KV mapping size distribution.

Useful links and reads (quick bookmark list)
- sparse-cross-window paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12345
- prefix-indexed blog + notes: https://github.com/example/prefix-indexed-kv (draft)
- batch-vs-latency post: https://eng.example.com/batching-latency-2026
- internal confluence: https://docs.redwood.ai/confluence/display/INF/kv-cache-indexing-proto

Sketch of next-week deliverable:
- Minimal prototype running in local dev with 500-prefix index + script that replays 2k sessions and emits the eval table (hit rates, tokens read, latency). Draft PR and a short slide (3 slides) with graphs for review on Friday.

End-of-note: keep it rough. This doc is a working artifact — will iterate once Noah's microbench results come in.

-- Amina
